panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (a, b, c). a: H&E breast biopsy tissue from a patient with clinical calciphylaxis demonstrates basophilic intimal vascular ossification-calcification in a small musculoelastic artery, as specified by the caption. b: The panel shows H&E vascular ossification-calcification with medial arteriolar involvement, a characteristic histopathologic manifestation associated with calciphylaxis. c: H&E breast biopsy tissue demonstrates basophilic adventitial vascular ossification-calcification in an arteriole, explicitly attributed by the caption to the systemic vascular changes of calciphylaxis.

panels.figure_caption: Histologic changes in a patient with CPLX and ESRD. Breast biopsy (benign) from a non-diabetic 60-year-old Caucasian female with an irregular breast mass 12 months prior to the development of clinical abdominal CPLX (multiple tumorous calcifications in the abdominal adipose tissue and skin ulceration). These tissue sections demonstrate the underlying systemic VOC of calciphylaxis. Her ulcerated area on the abdomen was not biopsied due to a possibility of aggravating tissue healing. Panel a: Demonstrates the H&E basophilic staining of intimal VOC in a small musculoelastic artery. Panel b: Demonstrates the medial fluorescent-like staining (due to inverted coloration of H & E basophilic staining) of VOC in an arteriole. Note the adjacent venule medial VOC staining. Venular VOC – thrombosis has not been as extensively studied as the arteriole and one must consider the possibility that VOC – thrombosis in the post-capillary venule may be important as the increased capillary edema and pressure may result in capillary endothelial dysfunction and promote an additive factor in the important role of subcutaneous ischemia and skin necrosis and ulceration. Note the panarteriolar involvement of the intima, media, and adventitia in the various vessels. Panel c: Demonstrates the H & E basophilic adventitial staining of VOC in an arteriole.
in_text_mentions: VOC in the syndrome of CPLX – CUA is an important topic for discussion, as it is being reported at an exponential rate and especially over the past two years. The devastating complication of medial vascular calcification of small arterioles with resulting skin necrosis is rapidly becoming a morbid complication in both the non-diabetic and especially the large numbers of diabetic patients (T2DM > T1DM) undergoing renal replacement therapy (figure 7).

extremely high risk for the development of excessive medial arterial remodeling and VOC, as well as arteriole remodeling and VOC, which could possibly increase the risk of developing CPLX (figure 2, 7). Many T2DM patients may have medial arteriolar calcification that could be contributing to anunderlying skin necrosis currently being attributed singularly to peripheral arterial disease and ischemic necrosis or gangrene, when if fact they might have coexisting arteriolar calcification contributing to their skin changes of gangrene. plate_findings.evidence: Caption identifies severe calciphylaxis-induced skin ulcers on admission; the image shows extensive bilateral ulcerative, necrotic-appearing lesions.
Caption states that calcium deposits were present in the media of small- and medium-sized arteries; this panel is the hematoxylin-eosin-stained biopsy section.
Caption states that CT showed multiple subcutaneous and intramuscular calcifications in the thigh soft tissues; the panel is explicitly labeled vessel calcification on CT.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B1, B2, C). A: Clinical photograph of a human patient with severe skin ulcers attributed by the caption and article title to calciphylaxis. The lesions are large, irregular, necrotic ulcers on both thighs. B1: Hematoxylin-eosin histopathology from the ulcer showing the captioned vascular medial calcium deposits, a characteristic finding of calciphylaxis. B2: Von Kossa-stained section demonstrates vascular wall mineralization in a biopsy from a calciphylaxis ulcer, directly supporting medial arteriolar calcification. C: Axial CT of the thighs shows multiple calcifications in the subcutaneous and intramuscular soft tissues, as captioned, supporting calciphylaxis-associated vascular/soft-tissue calcification.

Calcium deposits in the media of small- and medium-sized arteries. c Plain computed tomography showed multiple subcutaneous and intramuscular calcifications in the soft tissue of the thighs
